title: Docker is weird (codeandcake.dev)
comments: Hi, I'm the creator of Docker and came across this post. It's always fun to see other engineers think about how you designed a system. I haven't been involved in developing Docker in many years, but it's a fun trip down memory lane.I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.reply

What was your thought process that made you think that these Linux primitives give the opportunity to make it a platform for distributing and deploying packaged applications and eliminating a lot of the issue around "it works my machine" argument?You may have already answered this somewhere, so feel free to tell me what to search for or if you have a link to hand, that works too :)reply
Docker was basically a commercialisation of lxc and now we got nspawn going full circle.reply

This is incorrect.Docker in its earlier incarnations was based on openvz, which predates lxc. The  lxc project was initially a kernel development project: a collection of kernel patches to add container support. The userland tool was just a companion. When it became apparent that these patches would "win" the race to be upstreamed even though openvz was much more mature, we switched our tooling to lxc. The patches matured over time, but the userland tool (what we now know as "lxc") was finicky.The original open-source release of Docker wrapped lxc for low-level container operations. But it was just too unreliable and we swapped it out for an in-house Go implementation called "libcontainer".As for "commercializing": Docker was famously bad at commercializing anything, we open sourced so much (maybe too much) and still people complained that we were not open enough.reply

“Docker was famously bad at commercializing anything, we open sourced so much (maybe too much) and still people complained that we were not open enough”Developers are a tough market to please, especially when your business revolves around open source software.Unless you have an option to do private cloud hosting (like all these databases and other platforms do), it’s incredibly difficult to monetize.In the case of docker, I think it’s in the nature of the product that it’s difficult to monetize. Best you can do is enterprise support contracts, but those aren’t good enough to justify all that VC funding.reply

I don't think it's necessarily that difficult to monetize, they just ignored a lot of the needs of enterprise users (rootless, not punching holes in the firewall, not fighting with systemd, private registries) for long enough that other projects (e.g. Podman, Quay) filled the void.reply
In the end, how were you able to monetize Docker?reply

first_paragraph: I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird. Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker.Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc.There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat.Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network.Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale (anthropic.com)
comments: I think somewhat of the opposite will actually occur. LLMs won’t formally verify LLM generated imperative style code. We (including agentic development) will move on from imperative languages, skipping functional and move to deterministic declarative languages.Likely, a proliferation of experimental languages all somewhat akin to Typescript for SQL with significantly more nuanced operators to tersely capture the same outcomes as imperative languages.They’ll compile down to be able to run performantly for game development or even for the Linux kernel (as if Linus would ever agree lol) but also they’ll be able to run on distributed execution engines with effectively a shared memory space, etc.Allows for significantly more terse artifacts. Lower chance of hallucination, fewer output tokens, fewer thinking loop iterations and concise enough for humans to review (for domains that need it).On top of that, additional theorem like syntax to drastically limit the ability of functions, etc. likely some sort of higher level effect system for verification. Used for many things like “constant time compilation for crypto functions”, and also “ensure acid compliance” for writes and reads in a local context, and things like “ensure only once delivery” for functions on a distributed execution engine.At which point every program will be formally verified by default. You could think of it as AdaErlangSQL+++reply

What you're describing is a language that can effectively take a high-level design doc (limited to a formal language representing a pseudo-English-subset) and compile to almost arbitrarily complex, formally verifiable systems. I say systems because you're also implying these could essentially orchestrate distributed systems.Which, if that were really possible, would be pretty good evidence of AGI. Or, at least, the end of 6-7 figure software engineer salaries. Conversely, I think it's a pipe dream. Writing a compiler that actually works well across such a broad range of hugely complex behaviors would itself be absurdly complex.reply

AGI will accelerate it, but way before agentic development I learned this was the future when I worked at Amazon. I no longer have access to the internal talks about it (amazing to watch) but here is a public link worth reading:https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/storage/how-automated-reasoning...reply

Also you would probably want to cache the compiler's output in git because running that compiler would take a long time, and you probably want the compiler's output to still be inspectable to human inspection. In the end that compiled artifact would look a lot like source code.I think Rust's success in the AI space shows how useful formal proofs are, as Rust provides something very similar to that. Both because it helps with the understanding of LLMs, as well as with trusting the LLMs are not violating any basic properties (like please no nasal demons if the user sends a buffer larger than the allowed amount).reply

Depends really. I tried some experiments towards a pretty uniform relational language for expressing ordinary logic, temporal logic, requirements etc. It does work, but there's some unexpected obstacles.You'd think performance would be easy to achieve because you'd just write clear, high-level declarative facts and LLM + good optimiser + proof certification system will get you there in terms of performance. But you'll be surprised that relational/declarative specification gives you so much behaviour 'for free' that choosing what to actually compute from those relations is a very deliberate choice. It starts to look like finding an imperative-like path of demand through the relations. It seems that you get exactly the same problems but one level up.reply

Coming at it from another angle, we have historically made distributed systems manageable / 'verifiable' with RTOSs which give deterministic scheduling and locking primitives. We know that a task's max duration is its uninterrupted duration + max duration of all higher priority tasks which could pre-empt it, and so on. Deterministic pre-emptive scheduling and locking alone could be enough to prove a lot of invariants without full temporal logic, and writing code in 'RTOS logic' might be more natural for humans/LLMs than the more expressive and powerful alternatives.reply

I've enjoyed embedding declarative syntax inside imperative languages, like LINQ and prolog as a dsl. The imperative code can express temporality much easier, and the declarative code allows you to throw that away when you don't want it.reply
I think it won't happen because people just care to much for performance. You already see this now. You see a ton of rewrites moving to rust even from higher level languages.reply

title: Quad9 (DNS Resolver) to Exit France (quad9.net)
comments: (context: I'm the CTO of Quad9 and am one of the people dealing with the lawyers)There is an understandable focus on "how are you going to block French users" when we have also claimed that geoIP blocking is insufficient for selectively denying resolution for certain names  - we understand this conflict, but we think it is energy spent in the wrong place.It is probable that we will use geoIP filters to block French users from our services after November 24. We could apply this same geoIP filter list now to selectively block French users from reaching the sites that we've been told to make unavailable. But this would corrupt our core premise, which is that the DNS is not the right place for this to happen, and if we comply within France to meet the requirement then we accept the worst eventual outcome for users and we still do not have legally perfect coverage.  We wish to first remain consistent with our core mission, and secondarily we must remain as close to compliance as we can to the legal constraints put upon us. By accepting the demands for blocking, we would admit that such demands are permissible within our mission - that we will act on behalf of companies (or others) to create ineffective and mis-directed regimes of content constraint.We would be admitting that we think this solves the problem - it does not.  We would be admitting that we will do this for an ever-increasing number of names - we will not.  We would be permitting these methods to be applied for more areas of filtering such as moral, religious, social, or political reasons - we must not.So we accept that there is the possibility that we will have errors in our blockade, but in this case (blocking French users) we maintain consistency with our stated mission of integrity of the DNS. We would rather there be a clear distinction made for users of our services: you get the DNS as you (the user) expects, or if Quad9 is forced to pollute the service with unexpected and arbitrary number of fragmentation demands, then we will not offer the services at all.The underlying issue is not ONLY that geoIP blocking is ineffective, but that the entire premise of any of these demands is inappropriately applied to DNS recursive resolution providers. We would hope that this discussion continues to be on the most fundamental of the disagreement we have with the outcome in this court case, not on the details of the technical implementation which have yet to be entirely decided and which can be tuned over time.reply

comments: I've been using iron proxy recently for a project I just started, it does network restrictions by domain etc with plenty of options, credential swapping and more.I have no affiliation with it, but it solved most of what I need in one go when I was stressing out about it.Only real problem remaining if you truly want to be able to trust agents is how to prevent data (in my case codebases the agent works on) exfiltration a la HF incident.We can restrict network to trusted domains, but there's always a chance an agent could be extra slippery especially if prompt injected and doing something like pushing data out a few characters at a time.In my case I'm also giving it gh access and having to deeply check things like: can it manage to fork public repos and embarrass us by submitting prs, could it open issues, etc.But that's kind of solved by proxying the heck out of gh rather than giving it direct (or wrapping it or whatever) for additional controls that gh themselves don't provide.I'm still musing over the "it could send data to an allowed domain in a way we don't expect that exfiltrates something"...reply
It seems like some kind of network logging would be useful? Even if you don't catch it, you'd want to know what it did.reply

Yeah agree.In other comments I've mused about capturing data to be compared to the secret dataset, I'm sure it'd be possible to hash or something so that the proxy/sandbox doesn't have the data but can check it, or because it's not an agent it can call of to the data store for that.Then you can just collect sequential blocks of data the agent sends out that match to sequences in the dataset. The longer the matching sequence the heavier it weights it. Single byte matches are almost always incidental, but individually sent bytes over time that line up with a n byte sequence in the source data is sus. And larger sequences of bytes send in one go that line up are immediately sus. If the weight ends up too high the agent is paused/walled off and an investigation called for.reply
I've toyed with the idea of MITMing all connections and blocking any that I can't decrypt, but too much software has pinned certificates these days. (Too much for me, not in general)reply

title: The Secret Life of Circuits is now in stock everywhere (coredump.cx)
comments: I've been browsing his free sample chapter on basic electromechanical devices[1], and I must say that it is incredibly well written. Take a look at his explanation of switch bounce:If you pry open a typical switch, you’ll probably find that its internals are quite complex. Inside, there might be a small spring-loaded roller that travels over a tiny hump or an intricately shaped metal leaf that “pops” when pressed firmly enough. The purpose of these mechanisms is to keep the switch firmly in place until sufficient force is applied, at which point it snaps immediately into the new position. This nonlinear behavior provides satisfying tactile feedback, reduces sensitivity to vibration and other accidental inputs, and prevents the switch from resting in any state other than “fully off” or “fully on.”The flip side of this approach is that once the mechanism gives in, things happen quickly: The contacts are pulled apart or slammed together at a considerable speed. Because metal is elastic, this motion produces some vibration that manifests as electrical glitches lasting from tens of microseconds to a few milliseconds. The effect is known as switch bounce.I know about switch bounce but I've never seen it explained so clearly. Usually electronics books will say "mechanical switches will bounce before settling" and will then describe a circuit or algorithm to deal with it. What's always missing is a plain English discussion of the why and how.[1] https://lcamtuf.coredump.cx/electronics/previewreply

> worked around these types of devices and their interfaces..This is not a problem of devices and interfaces. You are supposed to generate the wrapping key on the HSM itself. title: Why My Asus Laptop Kept Rebooting After Sleep and How to Fix It (idiallo.com)
comments: xxx
first_paragraph: Losing my work for years.Three years ago, I bought an Asus laptop, specifically the Zenbook Pro 17. It's a powerful machine and works just fine for my needs, but it had one problem that made me want to either return it or throw it out the window.I would work on projects for hours on end and close the lid when I was done. I haven't manually shut down a computer in more than 10 years. I only do so after a forced update or during a debugging session. So I would close the lid, and a couple of hours later I would open it back up. Instead of waking from sleep, the computer would start from scratch as if it had been turned off and the battery was nearly dead.That meant everything I had open was closed. I'm lucky that most of the applications I run can restore a previous session, but it was extremely annoying. I had a similar issue with my previous Asus, and I had blamed Windows for it. The computer often woke from sleep just so Microsoft could perform an update, which used up all my battery.

title: Mapping the Northern Sky (maps.com)
comments: Understanding what is in the sky and what's around it is a fun skill to have, you can always tell which direction is what, the time of year (in case you forgot) and the time of night, assuming you are looking outside frequently enough to notice the change. You can even tell how much time has past if you are in the same spot and have a point of reference (like in a hot tub facing a tall tree) using your hand to measure. You can use Stellarium on your computer or phone to help see what's up there as well as a planisphere to know exactly what is up today at your lattitude and where it is at what hour.reply

Studying the constellations and learning the sky is a great way to get a visceral sense of our place in the universe. When you can't tell one patch of sky from another, the brain doesn't need a fancy model for the reality of it, and you can go around with a kind of subconscious "flat sky" in your head. But when you start to piece the constellations together, and it all connects up around you, that's transformative. Space stops being something that's "up there", and becomes a thing that surrounds you. It's a strange sensation when it first hits you, and well worth the time to achieve it.reply

They used the stars to tell stories, make predictions, and even find their way.
